Assert.note: Both can be compiled out (Python -O, C# Release builds). Never use assert to validate real input — the check can vanish in production.
Assert.title: assert

AsyncDef.note: Both use async/await with the same cooperative model. C# async methods return Task/Task<T> (async void only for event handlers); a Python coroutine returns a coroutine object until awaited.
AsyncDef.title: async def

Await.note: Same keyword, same semantics. Difference is hosting: Python needs asyncio.run() (or a running loop) to drive coroutines; C# continuations are pumped by the thread pool or a SynchronizationContext.
Await.title: await

ChainedComp.note: Python evaluates the middle operand once; spell it out with && in C#. Amusingly, `1 < x < 10` in C# compares a bool — a compile error, which actually saves you here.
ChainedComp.title: Chained comparison (1 < x < 10)

Dataclass.csharp: record class Point(int X, int Y);
Dataclass.note: C# records are the closest match: concise syntax plus value equality. A Python @dataclass is still a mutable class by default (unless frozen=True); a record class is mutable too unless you use init-only properties.
Dataclass.title: @dataclass

Decorator.csharp: // No direct equivalent: use an attribute + middleware, or wrap the method explicitly.
Decorator.note: Python decorators wrap the function at definition time and actually run. C# attributes are inert metadata — they do nothing unless something reads them (ASP.NET middleware, proxies, source generators).
Decorator.title: Decorator (@...)

Del.csharp: // No equivalent: let the variable go out of scope; use list.RemoveAt(i) for items.
Del.note: `del x` just unbinds the name; C# memory is GC-managed so there is nothing to translate. To remove an item, use Remove/RemoveAt.
Del.title: del

DictComp.csharp: var d = items.ToDictionary(p => p.Key, p => p.Value);
DictComp.note: Python dicts preserve insertion order. C# Dictionary happens to preserve it in practice but makes no guarantee — don't rely on it.
DictComp.title: Dict comprehension

DictGet.csharp: var v = dict.TryGetValue(k, out var val) ? val : defaultValue;
DictGet.note: The TryGetValue pattern is the idiomatic C# equivalent — no exception on missing keys. Note Python evaluates the default eagerly.
DictGet.title: dict.get(key, default)

DictMerge.csharp: // No spread syntax: merge manually, right side wins on duplicate keys.
DictMerge.note: Python {**a, **b} merges with the right side winning on duplicate keys. C# has no equivalent syntax — loop and assign, or Concat carefully (ToDictionary throws on duplicate keys).
DictMerge.title: {**a, **b} dict merge

Enumerate.csharp: foreach (var (value, index) in items.Select((v, i) => (v, i))) ...
Enumerate.note: enumerate() starts at 0 by default (override with start=). The C# LINQ Select overload with (element, index) is the same idea.
Enumerate.title: enumerate()

FString.note: Nearly identical. The format mini-languages differ: Python {x:.2f} vs C# {x:F2} — look up each specifier instead of guessing.
FString.title: f-string

FloorDiv.csharp: var q = (int)Math.Floor((double)a / b); // NOT a / b
FloorDiv.note: Python -7 // 2 == -4 (floors toward negative infinity); C# int division -7 / 2 == -3 (truncates toward zero). They differ for negative operands — a classic porting bug.
FloorDiv.title: Floor division (//)

ForElse.csharp: var found = false; foreach (...) { if (...) { found = true; break; } } if (!found) ...
ForElse.note: Python's else on a loop runs when the loop did NOT hit break — the most misunderstood Python construct. C# has nothing like it; use a bool flag.
ForElse.title: for/else (else runs when no break)

GenExp.csharp: IEnumerable<int> gen = items.Select(i => i * i); // deferred
GenExp.note: Both are lazy, but a Python generator is single-use: re-iterating an exhausted generator silently yields nothing. An IEnumerable can usually be enumerated again.
GenExp.title: Generator expression

Global.csharp: // No equivalent: pass state as a parameter, use a field, or inject a service.
Global.note: C# has no module-level mutable globals; the nearest hack is a static field. Prefer passing state explicitly or injecting a service — globals make testing miserable in both languages.
Global.title: global

InOp.csharp: if (dict.ContainsKey(k)) ... // dict: keys.  if (list.Contains(x)) ... // list: O(n) scan
InOp.note: `in` on a dict checks keys (like ContainsKey). `in` on a list is a linear O(n) scan, same as List<T>.Contains.
InOp.title: in operator (membership)

InitSelf.csharp: public C() { ... } // 'this' is implicit, never a parameter
InitSelf.note: Python passes the instance explicitly as the first parameter (self); C# constructors have an implicit this. Never translate self into a parameter.
InitSelf.title: __init__ and self

IsOp.csharp: if (ReferenceEquals(a, b)) ... // or: if (a is null) ...
IsOp.note: Python `is` is identity and `==` is equality — the same split as C# ReferenceEquals vs ==. Gotcha: `is` on small ints/short strings can appear to work because of interning; never rely on it.
IsOp.title: is / is not (identity)

Lambda.note: C# lambdas look almost identical. Difference: a Python lambda is limited to a single expression; a C# lambda can have a full statement body.
Lambda.title: lambda

LateBinding.csharp: // Capture a per-iteration copy: foreach (var item in items) { var copy = item; actions.Add(() => copy); }
LateBinding.note: Python closures capture VARIABLES, not values: lambdas created in a loop all see the final value. Fix with a default arg (lambda i=i: ...) or a local copy. C# for-loops share the variable too (foreach was fixed in C# 5).
LateBinding.title: Late-binding closure

ListComp.note: C# LINQ is lazy until you call ToList(); a Python list comprehension builds the whole list eagerly. Like C#, Python 3 does not leak the loop variable.
ListComp.title: List comprehension

MainGuard.csharp: // Top-level statements or static void Main() — the entry point.
MainGuard.note: C# has no 'imported vs executed' distinction: code in a library never runs unless something calls it. The entry point is Main (or top-level statements).
MainGuard.title: if __name__ == "__main__"

Match.note: C# switch supports patterns and looks similar. Python case patterns destructure and bind (case [x, y]:); C# list patterns ([var x, var y]) come close.
Match.title: match statement

MutableDefault.csharp: void F(List<int>? items = null) { items ??= new(); ... }
MutableDefault.note: DANGER: Python evaluates default arguments ONCE at def time — def f(items=[]) shares a single list across all calls. C# evaluates defaults per call (and only allows compile-time constants). Always translate with a null default plus ??=.
MutableDefault.title: Mutable default argument

NegIndex.note: C# ^1 is a close match for a[-1]. But out-of-range SLICING never throws in Python (it clips), while C# range slicing throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
NegIndex.title: Negative indexing (a[-1])

NoneLit.note: None maps to null. None is a singleton (compare with `is None`); C# null works with == and with pattern matching (`is null`). Nullable reference types make nullability explicit.
NoneLit.title: None

Nonlocal.csharp: // No keyword: C# lambdas capture locals by reference automatically.
Nonlocal.note: C# lambdas capture outer variables by reference automatically (like nonlocal), and C# has no nested named functions, so the declaration keyword has no counterpart.
Nonlocal.title: nonlocal

Power.note: Math.Pow returns double, so x ** 2 on ints gives an int in Python but a double in C#. For integer powers, prefer checked multiplication or a loop.
Power.title: Power operator (**)

Property.note: Direct match — both give method-backed attribute access. Python's @x.setter corresponds to a C# set accessor.
Property.title: @property

RaiseFrom.note: C# chains via the InnerException constructor argument. Python `raise X from Y` sets __cause__ explicitly; a bare `raise X` inside except still chains implicitly, like C#.
RaiseFrom.title: raise ... from (exception chaining)

Range.csharp: foreach (var i in Enumerable.Range(0, 5)) ... // Range(start, COUNT)
Range.note: Enumerable.Range takes (start, count), not (start, stop): range(5) == Enumerable.Range(0, 5). There is no step overload — use a for loop or Where for steps.
Range.title: range()

SetComp.note: Straight mapping: both are unordered collections of unique values.
SetComp.title: Set comprehension

Slice.csharp: var part = items[1..3]; // C# Range, end-exclusive like Python
Slice.note: C# ranges are end-exclusive, just like Python slices. Slicing a Python list copies; C# [1..3] on an array also copies, while items.AsSpan()[1..3] is a zero-copy view.
Slice.title: Slicing (a[1:3])

StarArgs.csharp:
void F(params int[] args)  // *args
// **kwargs: use optional parameters, a Dictionary<string, object?>, or an options class
StarArgs.note: C# has params for *args. There is no **kwargs equivalent — prefer an options class over a dictionary.
StarArgs.title: *args / **kwargs

StarUnpack.csharp: // No splat at call sites: pass elements explicitly, or use named arguments F(x: 1).
StarUnpack.note: C# has no call-site unpacking — spell out the arguments. Named arguments (F(name: value)) are the closest thing to keyword arguments.
StarUnpack.title: Call-site unpacking f(*args, **kwargs)

StrJoin.note: Nearly identical. Difference: Python join requires every item to already be a str (it throws otherwise); C# string.Join calls ToString() on anything.
StrJoin.title: str.join()

StrRepr.note: __str__ maps to ToString(). __repr__ (unambiguous, ideally eval-able) has no C# equivalent — ToString() serves both roles.
StrRepr.title: __str__ / __repr__

Ternary.note: Same as C#'s ternary operator, with identical argument order: value-if-true first.
Ternary.title: Conditional expression (x if c else y)

Truthiness.csharp: if (items.Count > 0) ... // C# forces you to be explicit
Truthiness.note: Python treats empty collections, 0, 0.0, None and '' as false. C# demands a real bool, so the compiler forces the explicit check — a whole class of bugs disappears.
Truthiness.title: Truthiness in if/while

TryExcept.note: Python's else runs only if NO exception occurred — C# has no equivalent; put that code at the end of the try block. except matches subclasses, just like C# catch.
TryExcept.title: try/except/else/finally

TupleUnpack.note: C# deconstruction looks the same but needs a Deconstruct method or a ValueTuple of known arity. Python unpacks any iterable of matching length.
TupleUnpack.title: Tuple unpacking

TypeHints.csharp: int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;
TypeHints.note: Python hints are unchecked at runtime (unless you run mypy); C# types are compiler-enforced. Treat hints as documentation when translating and verify against real values.
TypeHints.title: Type hints

Walrus.csharp: // No direct equivalent: assign before the if, or use pattern matching.
Walrus.note: C# has no expression-level assignment operator as clean as :=. Restructure with a prior assignment, or use patterns like `if (Get() is { Length: > 0 } items)`.
Walrus.title: Walrus operator (:=)

With.note: Python's with calls __enter__/__exit__; C# using calls Dispose(). A Python __exit__ can suppress an exception by returning true — C# Dispose cannot swallow exceptions the same way.
With.title: with statement (context manager)

Yield.csharp: IEnumerable<int> Gen() { yield return 1; yield return 2; }
Yield.note: C# also has yield return and both compile to lazy state machines. Difference: Python generators have .send()/.throw() coroutine-style methods; C# iterators do not.
Yield.title: yield (generator function)

Zip.note: Python 3 zip() stops at the shortest input, like C# Enumerable.Zip, and both are lazy. Python's zip(strict=True) — which throws on unequal lengths — has no C# equivalent.
Zip.title: zip()
